Top of the Morning
 

Illustration: Aïda Amer/Axios
 

Climate Week in New York City used to be about reducing emissions. Now it's about increasing power to data centers.

  • Axios Pro reporter Alan Neuhauser has spent the past few days on the ground with execs and investors, in a futile search for actual climate talk.
  • What he's heard a lot about, instead, is bringing as much 24/7 electricity online as fast as possible. If that's via nuclear or renewables, great. If it's via fossil fuels, so be it.

Why it matters: Climate change remains a critical global issue. But it's being subordinated to AI demands, like so much else.

What they're saying: "Climate Week should be rebranded to Get Energy Faster Week," Tesla co-founder and Redwood Materials CEO JB Straubel said Tuesday during an onstage conversation at Axios House.

Zoom in: The power push is eviscerating due diligence.

  • The defining metric is "speed-to-power," or how quickly a new energy source can begin supplying a project or grid. Not climate impact or even long-term viability.
  • "I have never felt this much market pull for our energy companies," one VC told Alan. "Customers are so hungry for any kind of energy source."

By the numbers: Projected new natural gas-fired generation in the U.S. alone has doubled to 155 GW by 2035.

  • ExxonMobil, citing the buildout, just increased its global emissions forecast by 10%.

Between the lines: Climate-focused VCs are still backing zero-emissions technologies, but emissions levels are largely irrelevant for PE and infrastructure firms writing the biggest checks.

The bottom line: The race to decarbonize has been supplanted by the race to bring power online.
 
 
The BFD
 

Illustration: Maura Kearns/Axios
 

Barry Diller has withdrawn his $18 billion-plus takeover offer for MGM Resorts (NYSE MGM).

Why it's the BFD: Diller is an MGM board member who in June said that MGM is unlikely to realize its "full potential" as a public company. Now it's going to remain a public company, at least for the foreseeable future.

Investor reax: MGM shares fell more than 10% on the news.

The bottom line: "Diller has said the deal would give his company, which includes People magazine, Food & Wine and other publications, a hedge at a time when artificial intelligence is upending the media business. He said real-world experiences like casino visits or shows remain more insulated from AI, for now." — Jessica Toonkel, WSJ

It's Personnel

Final Numbers
 
Data: FactSet; Chart: Axios/Matt Phillips

Treasury yields are soaring today, with the 30-year Treasury bond climbing to its highest level since 2004, Axios' Matt Phillips reports.

  • The selloff started to accelerate after a sizzling early report on the September economy.
  • Wednesday's gain of roughly 0.15 percentage points in the 10-year Treasury yield was the biggest since April 2025, when President Trump's "Liberation Day" tariff announcement rocked markets.
  • This morning, the 30-year yield rose as high as 5.44%, while 10-year Treasury yields hit 5.13%.
